title: Acute Cholangitis
bottomLine: Cholangitis is infected obstructed bile flow. Fever, RUQ pain and jaundice are classic; hypotension, confusion or oliguria means severe disease. Antibiotics treat infection, but persistent obstruction may require urgent biliary drainage/source control.
recognize: Older/critically ill clients may present primarily as sepsis
differentiate: Uncomplicated biliary colic lacks systemic infection
Cholecystitis is gallbladder inflammation; jaundice/sepsis raises concern for ductal obstruction or cholangitis
assessment: Stone, stent, stricture or recent biliary procedure history
workup: Lactate and renal function in sepsis
management: Prescribed IV fluids and broad antimicrobials
Prepare for ERCP or other biliary decompression when ordered
medicationSafety: Antibiotic choice depends on allergy, renal function, cultures and local resistance
Antibiotics do not replace source control when obstruction persists
counselling: Explain why drainage may be required even after antibiotics start
followUp: Reassess perfusion, fever, labs and response after source control
examTrap: Calling a jaundiced septic client simple gallstone pain and focusing on analgesia only.
oneLinePearl: Cholangitis = infection plus blocked bile: antibiotics and drainage thinking.
sourceBasis: Emergency Care BC Ascending Cholangitis clinical summary

title: Acute Cholecystitis
bottomLine: Persistent RUQ pain with fever and localized tenderness suggests acute gallbladder inflammation rather than brief biliary colic. Jaundice, rigidity, generalized pain, hypotension or sepsis signals duct obstruction, gangrene or perforation and requires escalation.
differentiate: Biliary colic is usually transient and afebrile
Cholangitis adds jaundice and systemic biliary infection
Pancreatitis more often causes epigastric pain radiating to the back with elevated lipase
medicationSafety: Analgesia must not replace reassessment of worsening pain
Antibiotics do not replace surgical review for perforation/gangrene
counselling: Explain acute NPO/procedure plan and follow-up
examTrap: Treating persistent febrile RUQ pain as uncomplicated biliary colic.
oneLinePearl: RUQ pain + fever = inflamed gallbladder; rigidity or shock = complication.
sourceBasis: Canadian emergency and surgical biliary practice

title: Bowel Perforation and Peritonitis
bottomLine: Sudden severe abdominal pain with guarding or board-like rigidity is a surgical abdomen. Keep NPO, support perfusion, give ordered antimicrobials, monitor urine output/mental status and prepare for urgent imaging and surgical source control.
differentiate: Uncomplicated gastroenteritis should not cause a rigid abdomen or shock
Obstruction can progress to ischemia/perforation when pain, fever or peritoneal signs worsen
medicationSafety: Do not give oral laxatives or food in a suspected perforation
Analgesia should accompany, not replace, reassessment
counselling: Explain the need for urgent surgical assessment
followUp: Postoperative sepsis, nutrition and wound monitoring
examTrap: Giving a laxative to a rigid acute abdomen.
oneLinePearl: Rigid abdomen: NPO, resuscitate, antibiotics, surgeon.
sourceBasis: Emergency Care BC bowel-obstruction/perforation emergency guidance

title: Ostomy Complications
bottomLine: A healthy intestinal stoma is moist pink-red. Dusky or black tissue, no output with cramping/distention, uncontrolled bleeding, or high-output dehydration are danger signs. Correct pouch fit and peristomal skin protection are routine nursing priorities.
recognize: High-output ileostomy can rapidly deplete fluid/sodium
differentiate: High output differs from obstruction, which causes reduced or absent output with cramping/distention
Ischemia causes dusky/black tissue rather than normal red mucosa
workup: Imaging or surgical review for obstruction/ischemia
management: Optimize pouch fit and skin protection
medicationSafety: Do not give output-slowing medication when mechanical obstruction is suspected
Drug absorption may change with some ostomies
counselling: Teach when to call the ostomy/surgical team
examTrap: Calling a black stoma normal postoperative bruising.
oneLinePearl: Pink and moist is healthy; black, blocked, bleeding, or dehydrating is not.

title: Enteral Feeding Tube Complications
bottomLine: Enteral tubes can cause displacement, aspiration, occlusion, leakage, skin injury, intolerance and refeeding complications. Verify position by the approved device/policy method before use, protect aspiration safety, flush appropriately, and stop/escalate feeds with suspected displacement, respiratory deterioration, peritonitis or severe metabolic change.
differentiate: Diarrhea can arise from medication, infection or formula—not feed intolerance alone
Aspirated air is not universal proof of tube position
workup: Imaging when displacement or perforation suspected
management: Stop feed if position/aspiration safety is uncertain
medicationSafety: Do not crush enteric-coated or extended-release medication
Review tube compatibility and feed-drug interactions
counselling: Tube and site care, blockage prevention and when to seek help
examTrap: Using auscultated air as universal confirmation that a feeding tube is safely positioned.
oneLinePearl: Before feeding: right tube, right place, safe lungs, safe electrolytes.
sourceBasis: Canadian enteral nutrition and device-policy practice
